did_you_know.text: Did you know? Psalm 104 opens with the call, “Bless the LORD, O my soul,” and ends with nearly the same words—“Bless the LORD, O my soul”—giving the psalm a frame structure.

Did you know? At the beginning of the psalm, creation is described using images of clothing and kingship: the LORD “wraps himself in light as with a garment,” and the heavens are stretched out “like a tent curtain.”
Did you know? The verse “He makes his angels winds, his servants flames of fire” presents the winds and blazing fire as servants of God within the description of the forces of creation.
Did you know? The psalm emphasizes the earth’s stability: the LORD established it on its foundations, so it will not “be moved forever and ever.”
Did you know? According to the psalm’s description, the waters were given a clear boundary: they may not cross it or return to cover the earth.
Did you know? The psalm describes the earth as the source both of food for animals—“grass for the cattle”—and of human labor, from which “bread comes from the earth.”
Did you know? The sun and moon play a role in the order of time: the moon is made “for appointed times,” and the sun knows the place of its setting.

Did you know? The psalm places side by side the activity of the forest animals at night and human work during the day: when the sun rises, the animals retreat, and people go out to their work until evening.
Did you know? The sea is described as vast and wide, filled with countless creatures—small and great—and is therefore a central part of the picture of creation’s abundance and variety.
Did you know? The verse describes a cycle of life and renewal: when the LORD sends his spirit, creatures are created anew and the face of the earth is renewed.
